title: Machines and computation histories

based_on.title: Computability and Incompleteness
based_on.pages: 35–41 (§2.6, machine equivalence, primitive-recursive histories and search; version 2007-01-09)

based_on.title: Formalizing Computability Theory via Partial Recursive Functions
based_on.pages: 12:9–12:13 (§§4.2–5.2, paired recursive programs and resource-bounded evaluation; ITP 2019)

summary: Record a computation as numbered states, check its finite history, and prove that one search for such a history computes every partial recursive function.
abstract: A machine can run forever, but a successful run leaves a finite record that we can check one step at a time. We use a concrete model whose state is a natural number and whose transitions perform bounded arithmetic calculations. The functions computed by these machines are exactly the partial recursive functions. The proof works in both directions: finite histories let us express a machine run by recursive search, while evaluation with increasing finite allowances turns every recursive program into a machine. As a result, even a program with many nested searches can be replaced by one search for a finite certificate and a simple extraction of its output.
